en: The *Mīmāṃsā-paribhāṣā* composed by the venerable Śrī Kṛṣṇa Yajvan:
An Auspicious Invocation.
Salutations to the illustrious Veda-Puruṣa; I bow to Sūryanārāyaṇa and the goddess Tripurasundarī;
and I constantly worship my gurus who have realized the ultimate truth. || 1 ||
This *Mīmāṃsā-paribhāṣā* is composed by Kṛṣṇa Yajvan for the sake of the intelligent, so that the young may gain even a slight understanding of the meanings established in the treatises. (2)
The subject matter of Mīmāṃsā:

Here, indeed, in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* consisting of twelve chapters (*dvādaśalakṣaṇī*), the great sage Jaimini has investigated only *dharma* and *adharma* for the sake of their application in practice. Among these, *dharma* is that which is characterized by being a means to a desired end as taught by the Veda, such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like. *Adharma* is that which is characterized by being a means to an undesired end as taught by the Veda, such as the eating of the *kalaja* (heart-liver) and the like. The authorities (*pramāṇa*) for these two are the Veda, the Smṛti, and established custom (*ācāra*). Of these, the Veda is an independent authority; the other two, however, are so by virtue of being rooted in the Veda. The twofold nature of the Veda:

In this regard, the Veda is twofold: consisting of *mantras* and consisting of *brāhmaṇas*. Among these, it will be explained that *mantras* are employed as the cause for recollecting the ritual acts at the time of performance; "performance" (*prayoga*) means the actual execution, and "at that time" refers to the moment of such execution. A sentence that prescribes an action is a *brāhmaṇa*. Its supplementary portion is the *arthavāda*. It will be explained that its authority is established through syntactic unity with the injunctive sentence, by way of generating a cognition of the excellence of that which is to be enjoined.
These are the various types of *brāhmaṇa* sentences.

The statements concerning qualities (*guṇa*) and Brahmins are of many kinds, distinguished as: the originative statement of an action (*karmotpattivākya*), a [mere] statement, a statement of result (*phalavākya*), a statement of a quality for the sake of a result, and the originative statement of an action with its qualities (*saguṇakarmotpattivākya*), and so forth.
Regarding the originative statement of an action:

that sentence by which it is understood that "this action is to be performed" is an originative statement of an action; for example, "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Here, the *agnihotra* oblation is enjoined as something to be performed; thus, this is an originative statement of an action.

A "qualitative statement" (*guṇavākya*) is a statement that, once a ritual action has been enjoined, prescribes a substance, deity, or the like as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of that action; for example, "One should offer with curd" (*dadhnā juhuyāt*). Here, curd is prescribed as a subordinate element with reference to the oblation (*homa*); thus, this is a qualitative statement. The status of being a "quality" (*guṇatva*) for curd and so forth consists precisely in their being enjoined as subordinate elements of the ritual action. In this context, the "status of being the object of reference" (*uddeśyatva*) for the oblation means its being designated as something already established by another means of knowledge (*māna*), while being presented as that which is connected to the thing to be enjoined.

That which has already been established by another means of knowledge (*māna*) and is stated again possesses the character of being a restatement (*anuvādyatva*), as well as primacy (*prādhānya*) due to its connection with qualities such as curd (*dadhi*). Since curd and the like have not been established by another means of knowledge, they possess the character of being that which is enjoined (*vidheyatva*) in this very context; furthermore, because they serve as the instrument for the oblation (*homa*), they possess the character of being subordinate (*guṇatva*) relative to the oblation, and because they are to be performed by the person, they possess the character of being something to be undertaken (*upādeyatva*). Here, it should be understood that "being established by another means of knowledge" means being known through another means of knowledge, while "not being established" means being unknown. [This concludes] the sentence concerning the result.

When there is a desire for the fruit of an action that has already been enjoined, an injunction that makes known the connection with that fruit is a *phalavidhi* (fruit-injunction); for example, "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra*. Here, the sentence "He who desires heaven should bring about—that is, perform—the oblation named *agnihotra* as a means to that [heaven]" makes known the connection with the fruit of the action produced by the *agnihotra* injunction; thus, this is a fruit-injunction. A sentence concerning a subsidiary element (*guṇavākya*) is for the sake of the fruit.

A sentence prescribing a subordinate element for the sake of a result (*guṇavidhi*) is one that, depending upon an action already established, prescribes a subordinate element for the sake of a result—such as, "One desiring sensory power should offer with curd" (*dadhnendriyakāmasya juhuyāt*). Depending upon the oblation produced by the *agnihotra* injunction, the subordinate element in the form of curd is prescribed for the sake of the result of sensory power: "One should bring about the result of sensory power by means of curd which has become dependent on the oblation. This means "by means of curd which has become a constituent factor (*kāraka*) of the oblation. This very [injunction] is called both a "prescription of a subordinate element for a result" (*guṇaphalavidhi*) and a "prescription of a subordinate element for one who desires [a specific result]" (*guṇakāmavidhi*).
It is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) of a ritual act accompanied by a subordinate element.

A sentence that prescribes an action qualified by attributes such as substance and deity is a "sentence of originative injunction for an action with attributes" (*saguṇakarmotpattivākya*); for example, "One should sacrifice with soma. Here, a sacrifice qualified by the *soma* creeper is enjoined. Even in an injunction of a qualified entity, there is an injunction of the qualifier by implication.
This is a sentence of originative injunction for an action accompanied by its fruit.

In some cases, the very sentence that originates the ritual action also serves to communicate its connection with a result; for example: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. Here, a sacrifice named *udbhid*, already enjoined by another sentence, is prescribed for one desiring cattle as a means to the result of obtaining cattle. Thus, this single sentence alone prescribes the sacrifice as both the means and the result.
This is the *prayogavidhi* (the injunction of performance).

The principal injunction itself, having attained the status of a "great sentence" through syntactic unity with the subsidiary injunctions, is called the "injunction of performance" (*prayogavidhi*), because it prescribes the performance of the principal rite as qualified by all its subsidiaries; for example: "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra. Here, the meaning understood is: "One should bring about heaven by means of the Agnihotra oblation. That is to say, "one should produce [it]. In this context, the expectancy regarding the manner of performance arises: "How should one effect heaven by means of this oblation?"

Just as when it is said, "One should effect a division with an axe," there arises an expectation—"How should one effect the division with this?"—and it is understood that this is done by means of [actions] such as raising and striking; likewise here too, it is understood that "one should effect heaven by means of the Agnihotra sacrifice, assisted by the aggregate of subsidiaries—such as the carrying forth of the fire (*praṇayana*), the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*), and the purification of the sacrificial ground—which are enjoined by subsidiary injunctions within the context (*prakaraṇa*)."

The injunction of performance (*prayogavidhi*) is of such a nature that, by means of the sentence "for the sake of heaven," the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*) is enjoined. This entire collection of auxiliaries is called the "manner of being" (*itthambhāva*), as well as the "procedure" (*itikartavyatā*). In this context, the *agnihotra* oblation is the primary act (*pradhāna*), while everything beginning with the carrying of the fire (*praṇayana*) is an auxiliary. [Thus] there is the postulation of a result-apūrva (*phalāpūrva*).

If it be objected that this is untenable—since it is impossible for actions that perish very quickly to be the means of accomplishing results such as heaven that occur at a later time—we say: not so. Once it is understood from various scriptural injunctions and prohibitions that specific prescribed and forbidden actions are the means to their respective fruits, one postulates an *apūrva* (unseen potency) in the form of merit or demerit as an intermediate state. This is done to account for how actions that perish immediately can serve as the means to results occurring at a later time. Consequently, sacrifices and the like are the means to heaven by way of the *apūrva*, not directly.

That alone is the *phalāpūrva* (the apūrva resulting from the fruit). And its status as the instrument belongs to the principal rite (*pradhāna*) as qualified by its preceding and succeeding auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), not to the principal rite alone. For if the *phalāpūrva* were produced from the principal rite alone, the fruit would be accomplished from that very source, which would result in the futility (*ānarthakya*) of the auxiliary rites. [Thus,] the postulation of the *utpattyapūrva* (the apūrva of production) is necessary.

If it is objected that it is improper for the principal act (*pradhāna*), which is qualified by all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), to produce [the result] beforehand—since this is impossible because the principal act, being rapidly perishable, lacks simultaneity with its parts—the answer is no; for even though the principal action lacks simultaneity with the parts in its own essential form, such simultaneity is possible through the mediation of the "unseen potency of production" (*utpattyapūrva*).

In order to establish the concomitance of all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) with the principal act (*pradhāna*), it is accepted that there exists a certain *apūrva* called "origination" (*utpatti*), produced by the principal act alone, occurring between the principal act and the supreme *apūrva*. Likewise, since the auxiliaries also assist the principal act only when combined with one another, and because they lack concomitance in their own essential forms (*svarūpa*), their concomitance must be understood as being mediated by their respective origination-*apūrvas*.

The so-called "subsidiary assistance to the principal" consists precisely in the activation of the principal's capacity to produce the *phalāpūrva* (the unseen potency resulting from the fruit). Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, however, there is this distinction: the Āgneya sacrifice is enjoined by the rule, "That which belongs to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, is never omitted on the new moon day and the full moon day"; the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice is enjoined by the rule, "With those two, he offered this [cake] for Agni-Soma on eleven potsherds at the full moon"; and the Upāṃśuyāja is enjoined by the rule, "He performs the Upāṃśuyāja in between."

The two [deities] Agni and Soma said, "One should sacrifice to us two with clarified butter (ājya) in a low voice (upāṃśu) at the Full Moon (paurṇamāsī). Because of this sentence, [the upāṃśuyāja] is enjoined for the Full Moon. These are the principal rites of the Full Moon. Taking as the cause the connection with the time of the Full Moon understood from their respective sentences, there is a restatement (anuvāda) by means of the word *paurṇamāsī*—which is singular in number and functions as a collective—in the *vidvadvākya*: "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the Full Moon. Therefore, wherever the word *paurṇamāsī* occurs in the Veda, there the collective group beginning with the Āgneya [offering] is presented.
Even though the word "sacrifice" (yajati) is not heard [in this specific sentence], there is indeed an injunction for a sacrifice.

If it is asked, "How can it be an injunction for a sacrifice when the word denoting a sacrifice is not heard in the sentence 'That which belongs to Agni' (yad āgneyam)?"—do not say so. The word "āgneya" is a derivative formed with a *taddhita* suffix prescribed in the sense that "Agni is the deity of this sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśa*). Through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "puroḍāśa," the relationship between the substance and the deity is understood.

That [connection] cannot exist apart from a sacrifice, because the relationship between a substance and a deity is impossible in any action other than a sacrifice; therefore, that connection must be stated as occurring only within the act of sacrificing, since the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity is accepted as being the very nature of a sacrifice.

Therefore, a sacrifice inferred from the relationship between the heard substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*) is enjoined by the postulated verbal form "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), as follows: "By means of a sacrifice to be performed at times such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), which has Agni as its deity and *puroḍāśa* as its substance, one should bring about the desired result. Thus, wherever only the relationship between substance and deity is heard—as in "One should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya" (*sauryaṃ caruṃ nirvapet*)—there too a sacrifice inferred from the relationship between the deity Sūrya and the substance *caru* is enjoined; hence there is no fault whatsoever.
Even in the absence of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers, there is injunctive force.

If it is objected: "Even though the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is heard in the sentence concerning the *upāṃśuyāja*, how can it possess injunctive force in the absence of an injunctive suffix such as the optative (*liṅ*)?"—it is not so; for the injunctive force is possible through the modification of the form *yajati* into *yajeta*. In the same way, the modification should be understood in cases such as *vrīhīn prokṣati* ("he sprinkles the rice") and *samidho yajati* ("he sacrifices the fuel-sticks"). Some, however, say that the injunctive force is possible by accepting that the form *yajati* is in the fifth mood (*leṭ*).

Likewise, the two Sāṃnāyya sacrifices enjoined by the sentences "The curd for Indra on the new moon day" and "The milk for Indra on the new moon day," as well as the Āgneya sacrifice enjoined by the sentence "That which belongs to Agni," are the primary rites on the new moon day. These three are referred to collectively by the name "new moon day" (amāvāsyām), in the singular accusative case, in the sentence: "He who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice on the new moon day."

Therefore, wherever the word ‘darśa’ or the word ‘amāvāsyā’ is heard in the Veda, there is the presentation of a collection of sacrifices (*yāgasamudāya*). The purpose of restating each triad of sacrifices collectively by means of the terms ‘amāvāsyā’ and ‘paurṇamāsī’ in the *vidvadvākya* (the sentences containing the term ‘vidvān’) is to justify the use of the dual number in such injunctions as ‘one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the darśapūrṇamāsa’ (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*). Otherwise, since there are six sacrifices—the Āgneya and the others—the plural form ‘darśapūrṇamāsaiḥ’ would have been required.

Reiteration (*anuvāda*) is the restatement of a matter already established by another means of knowledge. Likewise, the *prayāja*, *ājyabhāga*, *anuyāja*, and other rites mentioned in proximity to the fruit-bearing *āgneya* and other sacrifices are subsidiary (*aṅga*) to those six sacrifices;
they do not produce a separate apūrva for each triad.

This being the case, the meaning of the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta*) is as follows: one should produce the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of heaven by means of the two groups [of rites], the New and Full Moon sacrifices, acting in mutual conjunction. In that regard, when the question arises as to how there can be mutual conjunction between two groups existing at two different times, it is said that although there is no conjunction in their own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*), a distinct *apūrva* is produced for each triad of constituent acts; through these [intermediate *apūrvas*], the conjunction of the two groups is expressed.

When the question arises as to how each individual triad can produce the *apūrva* (unseen potency), it is stated that each individual triad—characterized by the entire collection of preliminary and subsequent auxiliary rites such as the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* sacrifices—produces the *samudāyāpūrva* (the collective unseen potency). Since the coexistence of all auxiliaries within a single triad is not possible in its own form, three *apūrvas* are produced through the three sacrifices; it is by means of these that the coexistence of all auxiliaries is realized.

Since even the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), such as the *prayāja* offerings, lack a concomitance with the principal acts by virtue of their own nature, their concomitance must be stated as occurring through the intermediate *apūrva*s (unseen potencies) produced by each of them. Thus, the very concomitance that exists between the *utpattyapūrva*s generated by the principal acts and the *utpattyapūrva*s generated by the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries is precisely what constitutes the "endowed-with-auxiliaries" (*sāṅga*) status of the principal acts, in the sense of being qualified by their subsidiaries.

And thus, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), by means of the three *apūrvas* produced by the Āgneya and other [principal rites], assisted by the *utpattyapūrvas* (origination-*apūrvas*) produced by the *prayāja* and other [auxiliaries], one single *samudāyāpūrva* (collective-*apūrva*) is generated. Likewise, on the new moon day (*darśa*), by means of the three *apūrvas* produced by the two [rites] dedicated to Agni and Indra, assisted by the *aṅgotpattyapūrvas*, one single *trikāpūrva* is generated. From those two *trikāpūrvas*—which are themselves produced by the triad of *utpattyapūrvas* belonging to the Āgneya and others—the great *apūrva* (*mahāpūrva*), also called the *phalāpūrva* (fruit-*apūrva*), which brings about the fruit, is generated. And from that...

Regarding the term "fruit" (*phala*): thus, it is established that the *prayogavidhi* (performance injunction) is the injunction that makes known the necessity of performing the primary rite along with its subsidiaries in order to bring about the production of the fruit-apūrva—namely, that "one should effect heaven by means of the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices assisted by all their constituent parts through the medium of the apūrva. Furthermore, injunctions are of three kinds: the *apūrvavidhi* (original injunction), the *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction), and the *parisaṃkhyāvidhi* (exclusive injunction).

The *apūrvavidhi* (original injunction): Among these, that injunction which brings about an object that is absolutely unestablished is an *apūrvavidhi*, such as "He sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). In the absence of this injunction, the sprinkling of the rice-grains belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices would not be established by any means whatsoever. However, when this injunction exists, the sprinkling is indeed established for those rice-grains connected with it; thus, because it brings about the sprinkling which was absolutely unestablished, this is an *apūrvavidhi*. The *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction) [is defined as follows]...

And that which restricts a matter already established as an alternative is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), such as in that very context: "One threshes the rice. In the absence of this injunction, since the rice used in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices must achieve the state of dehusking—which is conducive to producing the rice grains required for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—as understood from the original prescriptive statement, it might occasionally result in the tearing open [of the husks] with fingernails instead of threshing. In that case, because threshing would not have been established as an option, its performance would be rendered unnecessary by other means; thus, there would be only an occasional (optional) establishment of threshing.

However, since this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)—meaning that while this procedure exists, the removal of husks must be accomplished by threshing alone—it follows that splitting is entirely excluded. It should not be argued that the restriction to threshing is useless because the removal of husks can also be achieved by splitting with the fingernails, as there would then be no purpose for it; for one must accept a "restrictive unseen merit" (*niyamādṛṣṭa*), on the grounds that an unseen result is produced when the removal of husks is performed specifically by means of threshing. This is because the unseen merit arises from the restriction itself, even if the visible purpose is not thereby obtained.

And that *apūrva* (unseen potency) is utilized for the *phalāpūrva* (the unseen potency of the fruit) by means of the *yāgotpattyapūrva* (the unseen potency of the production of the sacrifice); therefore, because of the conceptualization that in the absence of the *niyamāpūrva* (the unseen potency of the restriction), the *phalāpūrva* itself would not arise, the *niyamāpūrva* is not redundant. This should be understood likewise regarding the restriction of the *soma* sacrifice and so forth.
[Now follows] the *parisaṃkhyā-vidhi* (exclusive injunction).

A restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) is an injunction that, when two options are simultaneously applicable, results in the exclusion of the other—such as the injunction of a mantra in the section on the *cayana* sacrifice: "He takes up the horse's halter with the mantra, 'I have grasped this rein of immortality. For in the absence of this injunction, the mantra, which reveals the act of taking up a rein, would apply to the taking up of the donkey's halter as well as the horse's halter, due to the indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting in its capacity to reveal the act of taking up a rein.

In this rule, one should take up the horse’s halter with this mantra and not the donkey’s halter; however, that [donkey’s halter] is to be taken silently, so there is an exclusion of the mantra regarding the donkey’s halter. Since both [the horse’s and donkey’s halters] would otherwise be obtained together, this is a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) whose purpose is the exclusion of the other. This should be understood similarly in cases such as "five five-nailed animals are to be eaten.
The six means of proof (pramāṇas) are: direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth.

Previously, the status of the *prayāja* offerings and others as subsidiaries (*aṅga*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) was stated. Regarding that, there are six means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that convey subsidiarity, distinguished as: direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*). The example of direct statement (*śruti*): In the case of "one should offer with curd" (*dadhnā juhuyāt*), the act of offering already established by the Agnihotra injunction is indicated by the word "juhuyāt"; then, by the direct statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*), curd is enjoined as its instrument. Thus, the subsidiarity of the curd is established through direct statement. The example of indicative mark (*liṅga*): An indicative mark (*liṅga*) is functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).

And that [indicative power] is of two kinds: residing in the object (*arthagata*) and residing in the word (*śabdagata*). The first is as follows: although in the injunction "he cuts with the *sruva* spoon" there is an understanding of the *sruva* being subsidiary to the general act of cutting (*avadāna*), its status as a subsidiary to the specific cutting of liquid substances such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and the *saṃnāyya* offering is due to its *liṅga* in the form of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*); for it is impossible to perform the cutting of a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and the like with a *sruva* spoon. *Liṅga* residing in the word, however, is the capacity to manifest the meaning.

Just as the mantra "I offer thee, acceptable to Agni" (agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi) is an auxiliary to the act of offering (nirvāpa) by virtue of its *liṅga*—that is, its capacity to manifest that act; for whatever mantra has the capacity to manifest a particular action, it is an auxiliary to that action. Similarly, the mantra "I cut the sacrificial grass, the seat of the gods" (barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi) has the capacity to manifest the cutting of the *barhis*; thus, by virtue of its *liṅga*—namely, its verbal capacity—it is an auxiliary to the cutting of the *darbha* grass.

The illustration of sentence (*vākya*) is the co-occurrence of other words; for example, "He cuts [the branch] with the mantra 'For sap thee' (*īṣe tvā*). Here, by means of the sentence, the mantra "For sap thee" is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the act of cutting. Alternatively, in the case of "To Agni, thee, agreeable," the words beginning with "To Agni, thee, agreeable" attain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the word "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*), and thus they constitute a subordinate element of the offering (*nirvāpa*).
The illustration of context (*prakaraṇa*)...

Context (*prakaraṇa*) means mutual expectancy—as in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Here, when it is stated, "One should effect the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of heaven by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," an expectancy arises: "How is the unseen potency of heaven to be effected by these two?"

Similarly, in proximity to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices which possess results, the *prayāja*s and other rites—such as "he offers the *samidh*s," "he offers to *tanūnapāt*," and "he offers the two *ājyabhāga*s"—are heard of as being themselves devoid of results. Since no result is heard of for them within their own sentences, there arises an expectancy for a purpose: "What is the purpose of these? Consequently, while the *prayāja*s and others have an expectancy for a purpose and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have an expectancy for the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāva*), the subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*) of all the *prayāja*s and others to the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is determined by means of *prakaraṇa*, characterized by mutual expectancy.
The illustration of position (*sthāna*):

"Position" means proximity; for example, because the mantra "śundhadhvam" (be purified) is recited in proximity to the vessels for the *sāṃnāyya* offering, it is an auxiliary to the sprinkling of those *sāṃnāyya* vessels by virtue of that proximity.
An illustration of name (*samākhyā*) follows.

*Samākhyā* (designation) is an etymological name. For example, just as the collection of rites taught in the *Adhvaryu-kāṇḍa* is subsidiary to the Adhvaryu priest by virtue of the designation *Ādhvaryava*, so too, in the case of sacrifices such as "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni," which are designated as *kāmyeṣṭi* (optional sacrifices for specific desires), the application of mantras such as "ubhā vām indrāgnī" as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses occurs by virtue of the designation *kāmyeṣṭi-yājyānuvākyā-kāṇḍa*. Application (*viniyoga*) means connection as a subsidiary element. Regarding the relative strength and weakness when these [means of proof], beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), come into contact: [The rule is: Direct statement is stronger than indication; indication is stronger than syntactic unity; syntactic unity is stronger than context; context is stronger than position; and position is stronger than designation. Thus, the relative strength and weakness among direct statement and the others is established. When there is a conflict between two means of proof, the weaker one is set aside by the stronger. For instance, in the case of the mantra "barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi" ("I cut the grass, the seat of the gods"), although its application to the cutting of grass is established by the indication (*liṅga*) of the word "dāmi" (I cut), it is superseded by the direct statement (*śruti*) "barhir dāmi" ("I cut the grass"). Here, the word "grass" (*barhis*) is mentioned twice; therefore, the first mention is a direct statement, while the second is an indication. Since direct statement is stronger than indication, the mantra is applied to the cutting of grass. Similarly, in the case of the mantra "syonam te sadanam kṛṇomi," although its application to the act of preparing the seat is established by the indication of the word "sadanam" (seat), it is superseded by the direct statement "sadaḥ kṛṇuhi" ("prepare the seat"). Here, the word "seat" (*sadaḥ*) is mentioned twice; therefore, the first mention is a direct statement, while the second is an indication. Since direct statement is stronger than indication, the mantra is applied to the preparation of the seat. Likewise, in the case of the mantra "agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi," although its application to the offering to Agni is established by the indication of the word "agnaye," it is superseded by the direct statement "nirvapati" ("he offers"). Here, the word "offering" (*nirvapati*) is mentioned twice; therefore, the first mention is a direct statement, while the second is an indication. Thus, the relative strength and weakness among direct statement and the others is established. When there is a conflict between two means of proof, the weaker one is set aside by the stronger. For instance, in the case of the mantra "barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi," although its application to the cutting of grass is established by the indication of the word "dāmi" (I cut), it is superseded by the direct statement "barhir dāmi" ("I cut the grass"). Here, the word "grass" (*barhis*)

When direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof converge upon a single point, each preceding one possesses greater authority while each succeeding one possesses lesser authority. For example, in the context of the Agnihotra sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "With the verse *kadācana starīrasi*, one worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse."

In this case, although it might initially appear that the mantra is subsidiary to the worship of Indra by virtue of its *liṅga*—that is, its capacity to manifest Indra—it is established as subsidiary to the worship of Gārhapatya by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) of the instrumental case in "with the *aindrī*" and the accusative case in "Gārhapatya. Thus, the application based on *liṅga* regarding the worship of Indra is sublated. For *śruti* is inherently applicatory (*viniyojikā*).

It must be said that *liṅga*, however, becomes applicatory only by first observing the capacity to manifest Indra and then postulating a scriptural injunction such as "one should worship Indra with the *aindrī*"; but that [postulation] is not possible here.

Where there is no application by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), as in the case of "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) and so forth, there the indicative power (*liṅga*) indeed becomes the means of application by way of postulating a scriptural statement—namely, "One should perform the offering with this mantra"—after considering the mantra's capacity to manifest the act of offering, because there is no obstacle to such a postulation of scripture. This concludes the discussion on the relative strength of indicative power and the other means of application.

Likewise, in the case of "I prepare a pleasant seat for you" (*asyonaṃ te sadanaṃ kṛṇomi*) and "Sit upon that" (*tasmin sīda*), because the word "in that" (*tasmin*) depends on the meaning of the preceding sentence, there appears to be a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatva*); thus, by the authority of *vākya*, the two appear to constitute a single mantra. However, by the authority of *liṅga* (indicative power), they appear to be separate mantras; for the first possesses the capacity to illuminate the act of preparing the seat, while "sit upon that" has the capacity to illuminate the act of seating.

In this case, because indicative power (*liṅga*) is stronger than syntactical connection (*vākya*), *vākya* is sublated; thus, by means of *liṅga*, the determination is made that "syonaṃ te" is an auxiliary to the act of preparing the seat (*sadana*), while "tasmin sīda" is an auxiliary to the act of placing the oblation (*sādana*). On the strength of the single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatva*) between "syonaṃ te" and "tasmin sīda," one must first assume an indicative power (*liṅga*) consisting of some capacity for placing the oblation, however it may be construed, and then a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) must be assumed: "One should perform the placing with this specific mantra."

When the mantra "asyonaṃ te" is quickly applied to the act of preparing the seat (sadanam) by means of a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) inferred from the indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the perceptible form of the seat—the capacity of that mantra to convey further meaning is exhausted. Consequently, the inference of a *śruti* based on the syntactical connection (*vākya*) is obstructed because it would be too slow; thus, there is a sublation of *vākya* by *liṅga*.

In this manner, the sublation of context by syntactical connection, of order by context, and of name by order should be understood. Likewise, there is also the sublation of syntactical connection and the others by direct statement (*śruti*). Thus, the means of knowledge that indicate subsidiary status (*aṅgatva*), beginning with direct statement, have been defined. [Now follows] the definition of a subsidiary (*aṅga*).

That status of being a constituent (*aṅgatva*) is the state of being a subordinate (*śeṣatva*). That is to say, it is "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*). Being for the sake of another consists in being pervaded by an activity initiated with reference to another. Since the *prayāja* offerings and so forth are pervaded by the human activity initiated with reference to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they fit the definition. There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves, because they are not the objects of an activity initiated with reference to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; for no person ever initiates an activity directed solely toward the *prayāja* offerings. Thus, there are two kinds of constituents.

Those auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are of two kinds: those that assist directly (*saṃnipatyopakāraka*) and those that assist remotely (*ārādupakāraka*). Those auxiliaries which, either directly or indirectly, produce the body of the principal sacrifice and, by means of that, contribute to the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of its production, are those that assist directly; for example, substances such as rice and the like, as well as actions associated with them such as threshing and sprinkling, and deities such as Agni and the like, as well as actions associated with them such as the recitation of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses.

In this context, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) [serves] by way of producing a transcendental excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the deity; whereas threshing (*avahanana*) and so forth [serve] by way of visible means such as the removal of husks. Rice-grains (*vrīhi*) and the like produce the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) by way of being ground into flour, and through that, they become the cause for the body of the sacrifice and its originating apūrva. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses [serve] by way of purifying the deity, and the deity itself directly effects the accomplishment of the body of the sacrifice, and through that, becomes useful for the originating apūrva.

Since a sacrifice consists in the relinquishment of a substance for the sake of a deity, and according to the established doctrine that "the very nature of a sacrifice consists in the substance and the deity," these [actions] are called *sāmavāyika* (integral). The *ārādupakāraka* (indirectly beneficial) actions are those which produce an *apūrva* (unseen potency) inherent in the self—such as the *prayāja*, *ājyabhāga*, and *anuyāja* offerings. These do not produce a refinement (*saṃskāra*) residing in the substance or the deity; rather, they produce an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the self, and are thus termed *ārādupakāraka*. This is the twofold classification of ritual acts.

In this regard, action (*karma*) is generally of two kinds: primary action (*arthakarma*) and secondary action (*guṇakarma*). Regarding the definition of primary action: therein, an action that produces an unseen potency (*apūrva*) residing in the self is primary action—such as the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Prayāja offerings, and so forth. Regarding the twofold nature of secondary action: secondary action is that which produces a refinement (*saṃskāra*). It is of two types: that which refines what has been used (*upayuktasaṃskāraka*), and that which refines what is about to be used (*upayokṣyamāṇasaṃskāraka*).
Regarding the *upayuktasaṃskāraka* (disposal of what has been used):

therein, *upayuktasaṃskāraka* refers to the rite of disposal (*pratipattikarman*). According to the definition: "Disposal (*pratipatti*) is the casting of a substance that has been used—that is, one whose purpose has been fulfilled—into a prescribed place. Examples include the consumption of the *iḍā* portion, the throwing away of the black antelope horn, the oblation of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: since the consumption of the *iḍā* consists in the disposal of the scattered portions of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) used in the primary sacrifice, it is appropriate that it be considered a *pratipatti* (disposal rite). However, how can the *homa* (oblation) be a *pratipatti*, given that it does not serve to purify a substance already used in the sacrifice? For the *homa* occurs simultaneously with the sacrifice, and thus the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) and so forth, which would be the objects purified by the *homa*, have not yet been "used" [in the sense of having completed their function]. To this, they reply: A *pratipatti* is merely a purification of what has been used; it does not require that the thing be used in the primary sacrifice itself.

If that were the case, it would follow that the disposal of blood and excrement—which must be performed at the time of extracting the omentum, heart, and other parts immediately after the immolation of the animal—would not be a *pratipatti* (disposal), because it does not consist of the casting away of a substance already employed in a sacrifice. Likewise, the throwing away of the black antelope horn (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇāprāsana*) would also not be a *pratipatti*, because even though it was used for scratching as an auxiliary to the sacrifice, it was not employed in the sacrifice itself.

Therefore, where merely the utility of speech is intended, there is utility here as well, since the dung and blood belonging to the animal—which has been utilized by the extraction of the omentum, the heart, and so forth—and which has smeared the hands, require a disposal (*pratipatti*). Thus, utility exists in some way even in the case of an oblation (*homa*). For instance, disposal is threefold: subsequent to the principal rite (*pradhāna*), simultaneous with the principal rite, and prior to the principal rite. Among these, the first consists of the consumption of the *iḍā* portion and so forth.

The second [type of] injunction concerns the *homa* (oblation) and so forth. For instance, it is heard in the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice: "He spreads [the base] once," "he cuts off two portions of the oblation," "he sprinkles [clarified butter] once," and "he offers the fourfold portion. In that regard, in the sentence concerning the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), the substance consisting of the fourfold portion is not enjoined as the means for the *homa*, because the *homa* itself has not been previously established and thus cannot be referred to by way of restatement (*anuvāda*). Nor is the *homa* obtained from the sentence "what he offers" (*yad ānāti*); for that sentence is an injunction of the *yāga* (sacrifice).

Nor should it be said that there is no difference between *yāga* and *homa*; for the meaning of the word *yāga* is the relinquishment of a substance with reference to a deity, whereas the meaning of the word *homa* is the act of throwing [the substance] into the fire. In this context, although the sacrifice (*yāga*) is already established by the injunction regarding the *Āgneya* [offering], the act of throwing cannot be restated (as an *anuvāda*) because it has not been previously established by implication. Rather, the act of throwing is enjoined by the statement "he offers" (*juhoti*) as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), which is already established by the sentences concerning the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*), the double-cutting (*dviravadāna*), and the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).

And that *saṃskāra* (consecratory act) is indeed of the nature of a *pratipatti* (disposal). This is because, based on such instructions as "I sprinkle [the cake] for Agni, who is pleased," the act of throwing a portion (*avadāna*)—which is a part of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) that has been somehow utilized for the sake of deities such as Agni as subsidiary (*aṅga*) elements—is appropriately a *pratipatti-karman* (act of disposal), since the cake requires such a disposal. Furthermore, this *saṃskāra* occurs at the same time as the primary sacrifice (*pradhāna*).

For, according to the injunction "The *hotṛ* offers when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered," the offering must be performed by the *adhvaryu* at the moment immediately following the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. Since the sacrifice itself—having been reminded by that very *vaṣaṭ*-utterance for the purpose of recalling the sacrifice—is to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) at that same moment, the simultaneity of these two actions is possible. This point is established in the *Vārttika* on the section concerning the "Offering of the Whole" (*sarvapradānādhikaraṇa*).

An instance of a preparatory act (*pratipatti*) occurring prior to the primary act (*pradhāna*) is as follows: "He throws out the dung" (*śakṛt saṃpravidhyati*) and "He discards the blood" (*lohitaṃ nirasyati*). This point was established in the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] titled "Because the animal is not immolated, the blood and dung are not objects of the ritual action" (*paśāvanālambhāllohitaśakṛtorakarmatvam*). These are the various distinctions regarding purificatory acts for things intended to be used (*upayokṣyamāṇasaṃskāra*).

The *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) pertaining to that which is to be employed (*upayokṣyamāṇa*) is also of many kinds: the *saṃskāra* of that which is directly employed (*sākṣādviniyukta*), the *saṃskāra* of that which assists what is directly employed, and the *saṃskāra* of that which is about to be employed (*viniyokṣyamāṇa*). Among these, the first is, for example: "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). This is the *saṃskāra* of threshing for the rice-grains that are employed by the injunction, "One should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhiryajeta*). The second is, for example: "One should touch the calf" (*vatsamālabheta*).

This is an instance of *saṃskāraka-vidhi* (an injunction for the purpose of refinement), as it refines the calf which assists the cow-substance directly enjoined as a subsidiary to the *dohā* (milking). The third type is as follows: "He pours curds into hot milk. Here, by the sentence "That is indeed the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas," the milk—which is to be employed as a subsidiary to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice—is referred to by the word "that" (*tat*). Since the pouring of curds serves to refine that milk which is intended to be employed, the pouring of curds is an injunction for the purpose of refining what is to be employed.

The *paśupuroḍāśa* sacrifice serves to consecrate the deities who have been used or are about to be used [in the animal sacrifice], while its element of renunciation (*tyāga*) has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In this regard, because the deities Agni and Soma have already been used in the *vapā* (omentum) sacrifice, they serve as the consecration for what has been used; whereas in the sacrifices of the heart and other limbs, they are yet to be used, and thus they serve as the consecration for what is about to be used. The *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice serves to consecrate both the substance and the deity as having been used, while its element of renunciation has an invisible purpose. The throwing (*praharaṇa*) performed with the *sūktavāka* formula is likewise the same.

Since the final fore-offering (*uttama-prayāja*) serves as a refinement for the deities who are about to be sacrificed to, it is a refinement of that which is to be employed in its own portion; in its other portions, however, it has an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose. Likewise, the fat-oblation (*vasā-homa*), performed prior to the sacrifice of the oblations such as the heart, is a disposal (*pratipatti*) in its own portion of the fat; in its other portions, it should be understood as having an invisible purpose.
