However, some say that the nature of a *pratipatti-karman* (concluding rite) is the state of being an action whose result is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) distinct from a refinement to be utilized later. They argue that since the substance consisting of four portions (*caturavatta-dravya*), having been reduced to ashes by the oblation (*homa*), cannot be utilized after the oblation, it is distinct [from utilitarian refinements]; thus, the definition applies to the oblation.
This establishes the primacy of the *arthakarman* (utilitarian rite) and the *guṇakarman* (subordinate rite).

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: in a primary action (*arthakarma*), the action is predominant with respect to the substance, while the substance is subordinate to the action; for example, in the *agnihotra* and similar rites, curd and other such items are subordinate. In a secondary action (*guṇakarma*), the substance is predominant and the action is subordinate to the substance. In instances such as "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) or "he threshes [them]" (*avahanti*), the predominance of the substance over the action is understood through the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), since the rice-grains are perceived as that which is to be accomplished by the action; thus, the action of sprinkling and so forth is subordinate to them. Furthermore, there are four types of secondary action.

Furthermore, the action of refinement (*guṇakarma*) is fourfold, distinguished as *utpatti* (production), *āpti* (acquisition), *vikṛti* (modification), and *saṃskṛti* (purification). Among these, *utpatti-saṃskāra* (the refinement of production) is, for example: "One should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīnādadhīta*). Although the Āhavanīya and other fires are already present within the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*), they are produced by means of specific mantras; thus, because it is the cause for the production of the Āhavanīya and other fires, the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*) is a *utpatti-saṃskāra*. *Āpti-saṃskāra* (the refinement of acquisition) is, for example: "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*).

The study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) is accomplished through the act of recitation; thus, this is a *prāpti-saṃskāra* (a preparatory rite for attainment). An example of a *vikṛti* (transformative rite) is: "One threshes the rice-grains" (*vrīhīnavahanti*). Since threshing produces a transformation in the form of the removal of husks from the rice-grains, it is a *vikṛti-saṃskāra*. An example of a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite) is: "One sprinkles water on the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*). [In this case, because the sprinkling produces a refinement in the form of an excellence within the rice-grains, it constitutes a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*) of the type known as *saṃskṛti*. It should be understood that among these, the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the study of the Veda (*adhyayana*) are independent subordinate actions and are not auxiliary to a sacrificial ritual (*kratvaṅga*). All rites such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), however, are subordinate actions belonging to a ritual.
The threefold nature of ritual action for a purpose (*arthakarman*):

Ritual action for a purpose is of three kinds—namely, the distinction between obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these, the *agnihotra* and similar rites, understood as being necessarily to be performed at the evening and morning times by a living person—as in the injunctions "One should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," "One offers [it] in the evening," and "One offers [it] in the morning"—are obligatory (*nitya*). The *pathikṛt-iṣṭi* and similar rites, such as "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pathikṛt," which have the occasion of the lapse of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices as their cause, are occasional (*naimittika*).

Regarding the non-performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, some maintain that there is indeed a transgression (*pratyavāya*), but no fruit (*phala*) results from their performance. Others, however, hold that there is a fruit in the form of the removal of evil (*duritanivṛtti*); for through such scriptural statements as, "By performing only the obligatory and occasional rites, one effects the destruction of evil," the cessation of transgression is heard to be their fruit. Nor should it be argued that, because they possess a fruit, these two would consequently become optional (*kāmya*) rites; for there is an absence of performance preceded by a desire for that fruit.

Furthermore, because there is no injunction in those respective ritual statements enjoining [the act] as a means to achieve that specific fruit for one desiring that fruit, its status as a "desire-based" (*kāmya*) rite would be untenable. Thus, desire-based karma is of three kinds.

Desirable action (*kāmya-karma*) is also threefold: that which has results solely in this life, that which has results in the next life, and that which has results both in this life and the next. Among these, the first is, for example, the *kārīrī* sacrifice. It is performed by one desiring rain as a means to revive withering crops at that specific time; it is not performed by one desiring rain at another time, nor by one desiring rain in a future birth. An example of that which has results solely in the next life is the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other such sacrifices performed for the sake of heaven and so forth.

Because heaven cannot be an object of enjoyment in this world. An example of a result common to both this world and the next is: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu"; such results as prosperity are explained in detail elsewhere.
Thus, the Veda possesses the capacity to make known supersensible (alaukika) objects.

If it is objected: "Since rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and substances such as rice (*vrīhi*) are perceptible and thus worldly, how can the Veda be a communicator of non-worldly (transcendental) matters? We reply: No; for although the rituals themselves are perceptible, their status as means for attaining fruits such as heaven is imperceptible. Thus, because the Veda—which teaches that a ritual must be performed as a means to its fruit—communicates a non-worldly matter in the form of "that ritual must be performed as a means to that fruit," it is indeed a communicator of non-worldly matters.

Thus, since the fact that rice and other materials serve as the means for sacrificial acts is not perceptible, there is no fault in the Vedic sentence that makes this known, as it conveys a supersensuous (alaukika) object. This is the manner in which an injunction functions as an enjoiner.

Now, the manner in which an injunctive sentence functions as an injunction is explained. In this regard, in the sentence "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), there are two properties in the *ta*-suffix following the verbal root *yaj*: namely, the property of being a verbal suffix (*ākhyātatva*) and the property of being the optative suffix (*liṅtva*). Among these, the property of being a verbal suffix is common to all tense-affixes; delimited by that [property], the optative suffix conveys the objective efficient force (*ārthī bhāvanā*), which consists of the activity of the person. This is the objective efficient force.

And that efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) is characterized by three factors—*what*, *by what means*, and *how*. To explain: in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is first understood through the suffix as "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*). This is because there is a rule that all case-factors (*kāraka*) expressed by nominal stems (*subanta*) must connect with the action denoted by the verbal stem (*tiṅanta*), and because the meaning of the verbal suffix holds primacy. Furthermore, since the meaning of the suffix has primacy over the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it is logical that the efficient force denoted by the suffix presents itself first.

Then he performs [the action]: because the root *bhāvayati* (to cause to exist/bring about), which has the same meaning as *bhū*, is transitive, there arises an expectancy for an object in the form "what should one bring about? In this expectancy, even though it is expressed by a different word, heaven (*svarga*) connects as the thing to be brought about (*bhāvya*). This means it connects as the object (*karman*) in the sense of being that which is to be brought about; that is to say, as the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). However, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), although expressed by the same word, does not connect as the thing to be brought about. This is because a sacrifice (*yāga*), being of the nature of suffering, is unfit to be an object in the sense of being that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*). Heaven, on the other hand, consists of bliss.

Because it is fit to be construed as the object (*karman*) by virtue of being that which is most desired as the self, the understanding arises: "One should bring about heaven" (*svargaṃ bhāvayet*). Then, when there is an expectancy for an instrument (*karaṇa*) in the form of "by what?", the sacrifice (*yāga*), which is presented within the same word, is construed as the instrument: "One should effect heaven by means of the sacrifice" (*yāgena svargaṃ kuryāt*).

Then, when there arises an expectancy regarding the manner of performance (*kathaṃbhāvākāṅkṣā*)—namely, "How should one bring about heaven by means of sacrifice?"—the collection of subsidiary rites (*aṅgajāta*) such as the *abhyanvādhāna* and the *prayāja* becomes connected as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), [with the understanding]: "One should bring about heaven by means of a sacrifice accompanied by both the visible assistance (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) produced by acts such as the *abhyanvādhāna* and *avahanana*, and the invisible assistance (*adṛṣṭopakāra*) generated by the *prayāja*s. Being the fulfiller of the expectancy regarding the manner of performance is what constitutes being a procedure (*itikartavyatātva*). For example, in the statement "One desiring rice should cook," the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) is understood through the optative suffix (*liṅ*).

When there is the expectancy "what is to be brought about" (*kiṃ bhāvayet*), rice (*odana*) is connected as that which is to be brought about; when there is the expectancy "by what means" (*kena*), it is understood to be "by cooking" (*pākena*); and when there is the expectancy "how" (*katham*), it is [understood] to be "by means of [cooking] assisted by fanning with grass. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence results in: "One should bring about rice by means of cooking (which is contact with fire) assisted by fanning with grass and so forth. The same should be understood in the case of the Veda as well. This is the verbal productive energy (*śābdī bhāvanā*).

That very optative suffix (liṅ-pratyaya), by virtue of being delimited as an optative, denotes the verbal productive energy (śabdabhāvanā) known as instigation (preraṇā). Even in the world, immediately after hearing a teacher’s sentence such as "Bring the cow," a student proceeds to bring the cow only after cognizing the operation known as instigation, namely, "This teacher is instigating me toward bringing the cow. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the cognition of instigation is the cause of activity.

Since it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the knowledge of an instigation (*preraṇā*) is produced by hearing the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, the capacity of the optative suffix and others for denoting instigation is grasped in common worldly usage; therefore, it is appropriate to postulate that very same capacity in the Veda as well. However, there is this distinction: in the world, the operation called instigation—which is conducive to activity such as bringing a cow—is a specific intention residing in the person who employs the command; but in the Veda, because of the absence of an employing person, it is accepted that this [instigation] resides solely within the words such as the optative suffix.

For this very reason, because it consists of an operation residing in the word (*śabda*), it is called "verbal productive energy" (*śābdī bhāvanā*). Because it is the cause of engagement with objects such as sacrifice (*yāga*) and oblation (*homa*), it is also called "instigation" (*pravartanā*) or "impulsion" (*preraṇā*). This verbal productive energy itself is also characterized by three factors. Among these, the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*), which consists of the person's activity, connects as the goal to be accomplished (*bhāvya*). The optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, as understood through study, connect as the instrument (*karaṇa*). The knowledge of excellence (*prāśastya*) conveyed by the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) connects as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

In this regard, the understanding of the verbal *bhāvanā* (verbal productive energy) is as follows: "Persons who have studied the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-veda*), who possess proficiency through their study of grammar, logic, etymology (*nirukta*), and so forth, and who—aided by the knowledge of commendation (*prāśastya*) derived from the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and other elements within the *svādhyāya* (Vedic text) they have mastered—should perform sacrifices and other rites as duties incumbent upon themselves. The phrase "they should perform" (*anuṣṭhānam kuryuḥ*) means "they should carry out the performance. Performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is activity (*pravṛtti*). Thus, it remains unimpaired that the activity of the person is the objective (*bhāvya*) of the verbal *bhāvanā*.

And this verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*), while being perceived in its own form within the individual injunctions such as those concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, is not perceived there as something to be performed; for in those cases, it is the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*) alone that is understood as the task to be accomplished. However, it is precisely in the sentence "One's own Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*) that it is perceived as something to be performed. Nor should it be argued that in this case too, it is the objective productive energy alone that is the object of the injunction.

This is because the verbal *bhāvanā* (efficient force) residing in every injunctive sentence is in fact nothing other than the objective *bhāvanā* (objective efficient force) contained in the statement "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*). To explain: the suffix *-tavya* is prescribed in the sense of the object after the root *adhi-iṅ* ("to study") preceded by the prefix *adhi*. And here, the object is the Veda (*svādhyāya*), which is the primary element; the act of studying, which serves to refine that object, is the subordinate action (*guṇakarma*), just like the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites that refine the rice-grains (*vrīhi*).

When the Veda (*svādhyāya*), distinguished by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of comprehension produced by study, stands in need of a purpose, its purpose is precisely the knowledge of matters such as sacrifices—which are useful for performance and are obtainable through the force of specific sentences containing injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth found within the Veda—because this is a perceptible result (*dṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, it is the means to worldly welfare (*laukika-śreyas*) such as heaven by way of the performance of those respective rites; for without the understanding of the ritual acts, their performance is impossible. It is not, however, an imperceptible (*adṛṣṭa*) result that constitutes the purpose.

Since a visible result is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible result. Thus, by the very injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*), all verbal productive energies (*śābdabhāvanā*)—as propounded by the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth contained within the injunctive sentences of the Veda—are enjoined as things to be performed, each characterized by its three constituent factors.

Men who have become proficient through the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (sāṅgaveda), having understood the necessity of performing sacrifices and other rites—which are productive of results—by means of the injunctive suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth contained within the *svādhyāya* acquired through study, assisted by the excellence (*prāśastya*) understood from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), would perform those sacrifices and other acts; that is to say, they would engage in them. "They would perform" means they would initiate activity.

In this regard, because the person's activity is construed as the objective (*bhāvya*), the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth understood from the study of the Veda are construed as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the knowledge of commendability (*prāśastya*) is construed as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, it is accepted that the verbal productive energy (*śabdabhāvanā*) also possesses a distinction of three factors, just like the objective productive energy (*arthabhāvanā*). Among these, even the manifestation of heaven and other desired ends as the objective is due solely to the force of the injunction (*vidhi*).

An injunction (*vidhi*) whose primary purpose is instigation (*pravartanā*) cannot compel a person to act if the sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth are not means for achieving a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, it brings about the status of being a means for attaining heaven (*svarga*) and other desired objects for the person toward whom the sacrifice—which is by nature an object of human activity—is directed. Otherwise, the injunction itself would lack its very essence as instigation, since instigation is defined as the operation that causes activity. However, in cases involving the *laṭ* (present tense) suffix and others, because there is an absence of the instigating element, there is no rule that the objective to be realized (*bhāvya*) in the objective-efficient force (*arthabhāvanā*) must be a human goal. This is the meaning of the term "efficient force" (*bhāvanā*).

The nature of *bhāvanā* (productive activity) consists in being the causal operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) of that which comes into being (*bhavitṛ*). In this regard, with respect to the objective productive activity (*artha-bhāvanā*), the definition applies because it is the causal operation of that which comes into being—such as heaven (*svarga*) and so forth—which is in the process of arising. With respect to the verbal productive activity (*śābda-bhāvanā*) as well, the definition applies because it is the causal operation of the person’s inclination (*puruṣa-pravṛtti*), which is that which comes into being. This concludes the demonstration of the status of words such as *jyotiṣṭoma* as names (*nāman*).

If it is asked: "In the statement *jyotiṣṭomena svargakāmo yajeta* ('One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma'), when the meaning is described as 'one should bring about heaven by means of the sacrifice,' how does the word *jyotiṣṭoma* connect [to the rest of the sentence]? The answer is: No, because it connects as the name of the sacrifice intended to be the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), in the sense of "by which sacrifice named Jyotiṣṭoma. If it is asked: "How is it its name? The answer is: By the etymological derivation that "the Stomas (hymn-chants) called *jyotis*, such as the *trivṛt* and others, exist in this [sacrifice]."

If it is asked by what means the connection of the sacrifice with the *trivṛt* and other *stomas* is understood, [the answer is] from another sentence: "The *stomas* are the *trivṛt*, the *pañcadaśa*, and the *saptadaśa*"; for the meaning of this word is understood as being connected to those [stomas]. In this way, the status of being a name (*nāmatva*) in various instances is to be understood through the reasons stated in the Śāstra, such as *tatprakhya* (being mentioned by that same name) and so forth.

Indeed, in the Śāstra, the status of being a name is established by four causes: *tatprakhya* (mentioning it by that very name), *tadvyapadeśa* (designation by that), *yaugika* (etymological derivation), and *vākyabheda* (splitting of the sentence).
Its status as a name is established by the principle of "being known as such" (*tatprakhyanyāya*);

for instance, in the injunction "one offers the *agnihotra*," the word *agnihotra* does not enjoin the accessory of Agni as a deity, because the deity is already obtained through the mantra enjoined by the sentence: "With the mantra 'Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā,' one offers in the evening."

However, there is another scriptural passage that proclaims fire—such as "Agni is light, light is Agni"—which, by taking as its occasion the connection with fire thus obtained, establishes through a *bahuvrīhi* compound that the term *agnihotra* is the name of the oblation (*homa*), based on the fact that the oblation is offered to Agni (*agnaye hotram asmin*). Nor should it be argued that since the oblation is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the *bhāvanā* denoted by the suffix, if it were named after that, the third case ending would have to appear—as in "by means of the *agnihotra*"—just as in the expression "by means of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. This is not so.

Since the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) itself signifies the instrument through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because of the principle that "that which is not established cannot be an instrument"—for it is impossible for something unestablished to function as an instrument—the use of the second case is justified either by its restating the state of being the object (*sādhyatva*) inherent in the oblation (*homagata*) as implied by the context. Thus, by the principle of "being known from that" (*tatprakhyanyāya*), this term is a name (*nāmadheya*).
Its status as a name is also established by the principle of "designation by that" (*tadvyapadeśanyāya*).

Likewise, in the injunction "one seeking to perform malevolent magic should sacrifice with the Śyena," the word *śyena* is the name of the sacrifice; it is not an injunction of a subordinate accessory (*guṇavidhi*) consisting of the bird Śyena as a part of the sacrifice. For otherwise, there would result the impossibility of the designation of a comparison between the standard of comparison and the object compared, as expressed in the passage: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey], even so does this [sacrificer] swoop down and seize his hateful rival against whom he performs the Śyena."

The designation, "Just as a hawk seizes another bird by swooping down upon it, so too this specific ritual action named 'hawk' seizes the enemy (bhrātṛvya) by swooping down upon him," is appropriate only on the view that it is the name of a ritual action. If, however, the hawk were enjoined as a subordinate element of the sacrifice, there would result a case of identity between the subject and the object of comparison (the hawk compared to itself), which is illogical. Therefore, because of the designation of its similarity to a hawk, the word "hawk" is the name of a ritual action.

Consequently, the meaning of the sentence is: "One who practices *abhicāra* (malevolent magic), desiring the destruction of an enemy, should bring about that *abhicāra* by means of the sacrifice named *śyena*. If it is objected: "Even so, since *abhicāra* is also mentioned in the Veda, would not even believers (*āstika*) engage in such malevolent rites? The answer is: No. Although *abhicāra* is mentioned in the Veda, it is not enjoined (*vihita*) by the Veda, because it is a result (*phala*). According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), a result is not to be enjoined; rather, it is the action itself that is to be enjoined as the means toward that result. Therefore, because *abhicāra* is [merely] mentioned as a result, its performance gives rise to demerit (*pratyavāya*). Its status as a name [of the sacrifice] is established through etymological connection (*yoga*).

Thus, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," the word *udbhid* is the name of the sacrifice intended to be enjoined for the sake of the fruit consisting of cattle; it is not, however, an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) consisting of the *udbhid*, directed toward a sacrifice already established in some way as its subordinate part. This is because a quality named *udbhid* is not well-known, unlike [qualities such as] curd and so forth. As for the sacrifice, it is the name of the sacrifice because the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is possible: "by this, the fruit is split open (*udbhidya*) [or brought forth]."

If it is objected: "Since the term *udbhid* can also be applied to a spade and the like by virtue of its etymological derivation—as in 'the earth is pierced (*udbhidyate*) by this'—why could it not be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the spade and so forth? We reply: No; in such cases, an injunction of a quality can never be asserted, because it would entail the fault known as the "conjunction of two sets of three contradictory factors" (*viruddhatrikadvayasamāveśa*).
This is the investigation into the two sets of three contradictions.

For instance: in the case of the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," since it is impossible to refer back (*anuvāda*) to a sacrifice that has not been established by any other means of knowledge, the sacrifice must be enjoined as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) whose object is cattle—namely, "one should bring about cattle by means of the sacrifice. Consequently, the sacrifice possesses the status of being enjoined (*vidheya*). Furthermore, because it is perceived as subordinate (*śeṣatva*) with respect to the fruit, it possesses the status of a subordinate element (*guṇatva*). "Subordinate" (*śeṣatayā*) means as a subsidiary part (*aṅgatayā*).

Because it is performed by a person for the sake of accomplishing a result, there is the quality of being "to be adopted" (*upādeyatva*). Thus, in the sacrifice, there exists one triad consisting of being "prescribed" (*vidheya*), "secondary" (*guṇa*), and "to be adopted. Likewise, in the injunction of the accessory *udbhid* with reference to the sacrifice, there is a second triad consisting of "primacy" (*prādhānya*), "being the object of reference" (*uddeśyatva*), and "being the subject of restatement" (*anuvādyatva*) relative to the accessory intended to be enjoined. These two triads are mutually contradictory; they would both apply to a single sacrifice. Therefore, this is not an injunction of an accessory.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," the word *soma* is accepted as having a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of a sacrifice possessing *soma*—thereby constituting an injunction of a sacrifice qualified by *soma*, namely, "one should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessed of *soma*"—so too, in this case, the word *udbhid* would constitute an injunction of a sacrifice qualified by the accessory *udbhid*, because it would involve a secondary signification in the sense of "that which possesses *udbhid*. This is not to be said, because [in the former case] there is no conflict among the three factors (*viruddhatrika*).

In the case of *soma* and similar terms, because there is no other way to interpret them, one must accept a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) by means of indicating possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). In the case of *udbhid* and similar terms, however, since it is possible to interpret them as names (*nāman*), it is improper to accept a qualified injunction. Therefore, by virtue of etymological derivation (*yoga*), terms such as *udbhid* function as names; they are names precisely to avoid the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Similarly, in the injunction "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," the word *citrā* is the name of the Prājāpatya sacrifice (due to the fear of splitting the sentence). In the passage, "Curd, honey, ghee, water, parched grain, and rice—these mixed together constitute the Prājāpatya," the relationship between the six substances such as curd and the deity Prajāpati is directly heard through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the phrase "that mixture is for Prajāpati. On the basis of this, the sacrifice inferred [from that relationship] is enjoined.

When there is an expectancy for a fruit regarding the sacrifice already enjoined, the sentence "One should sacrifice with the Citrā" serves to establish its connection with a fruit. In that case, since it is enjoined again as being for the sake of a fruit, and because that Prājāpatya sacrifice consists of various (citra) materials such as curd and so forth, the word *citrā* is the name of the rite. It is not the case that, having referred to (*anūdya*) the animal sacrifice already obtained from the sentence "One should immolate an animal dedicated to Agni-Soma," the two qualities of variegatedness and femininity are being enjoined by the word "should sacrifice."

When a ritual action (*karman*) already established by another means of knowledge is the subject of an injunction that prescribes multiple qualities (*guṇa*), there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). As it has been said: "When a ritual action is already established, more than one quality cannot be enjoined. However, when a ritual action is not established by another means of knowledge, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that a sacrifice—characterized by multiple qualities such as several deities, an eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa*), the new-moon day (*amāvāsyā*), and the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*)—is enjoined, being inferred through the relationship between the material substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*).

As it has been said: "Even many [factors] are enjoined with a single effort when they are not [otherwise] obtained. Now, just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), where—referring to the sacrifice already established by another means of knowledge—the injunction of the three factors (the substance of the animal, its gender, and its number), which are conveyed by the single word *paśunā* as subordinate members of that sacrifice, is accepted without syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); so too here, because there is the injunction of the instrumental factor (*kāraka*) consisting of the animal-substance qualified by the properties of variegatedness and femininity, all conveyed by a single word, there is no syntactical split.

For this very reason, since the animal (paśu) to be enjoined therein is something to be adopted (upādeya), the singularity inherent in it is intended as a constituent part of the sacrifice; thus, one must sacrifice with only a single animal. This is the established doctrine (siddhānta-pravāda): that in the case of "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the singularity is not intended because it resides in the object being referred to (uddeśya). How so? In "He cleanses the cup," the word "cup" (*graham*) is in the accusative case, and from this it is understood that the cup is the primary factor (*prādhānya*), as it is the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) and the purpose of the action.

The cleansing (*saṃmārga*), however, is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) with respect to each cup (*graha*). According to the maxim that "the subordinate must be repeated for each principal," once it is determined that "the cleansing applies to all cups, as many as there may be," there is no desire to know how many cups are to be cleansed; therefore, the singular number heard in reference to the object of the injunction (*uddeśya*), though explicitly stated, is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). If it were argued that this [singular number] does not belong to the object of the injunction but is itself something to be enjoined—namely, "one should cleanse the cup" and "that which one cleanses should be one"—[we reply: no.

If that were the case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the difference in the objects to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Furthermore, because there is no desire to know (*abubhutsā*) regarding [the number], and because an injunction is impossible [in that regard], the number residing in the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). However, even among the qualifiers residing in the subject, some are intended to be significant—namely, those qualifiers without whose significance the cognition of the subject itself cannot be fully established. For example, in that very same context, the "cup-ness" (*grahatva*) is intended to be significant; for without its significance, it would be impossible to know the essential nature of the subject.

Therefore, it is established that since the *camasa* cups serve the purpose of the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the *Soma* sacrifice—which is accomplished by means of the class of [Soma] vessels—there is no cleansing (*saṃmārga*) of them. In the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the animal is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) because it is enjoined in relation to the sacrifice. Since there is no repetition of the primary act for every subordinate element, when the question arises as to how many animals the sacrifice should be performed with, the singularity inherent in the enjoined object—conveyed by the singular suffix—is intended (*vivakṣita*), because it is what is sought to be known.

Furthermore, since the instrumental factor (kāraka) consisting of the substance "animal" (paśu)—which is qualified by gender and number and expressed within a single word—is the object to be enjoined, then by virtue of that animal being the object of the injunction, its gender, number, and so forth are also auxiliary to the ritual action; therefore, singularity is intended to be significant.

Alternatively, when gender and number—expressed by the third case-ending and thereby assimilated into the instrumental *kāraka*-power—are disregarded in their relationship with the nominal stem-meaning (the animal substance), and are instead enjoined as directly subsidiary to the action just like that [instrumentality], then a mutual connection follows subsequently according to the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*): namely, "the animal which is enjoined as subsidiary to the sacrifice is one and male."

Just as in the case of the injunction, "One purchases Soma with a ruddy, tawny-eyed, one-year-old cow," because there is a rule that factors of action (*kāraka*) must connect with a verb, the four qualities—being ruddy, being tawny-eyed, and so forth—are first connected as subsidiaries to the purchase of Soma by means of instrumental case endings, even though they are not mutually connected among themselves. Since an immaterial quality such as "ruddiness" cannot by itself be a means for accomplishing an action, it subsequently enters into a mutual, implied connection (*pāṣṇikānvaya*) with the one-year-old cow—the instrument of the action—as its delimiting factor: namely, that which is the one-year-old cow [is also ruddy].

That [word] *piṅgākṣī* (tawny-eyed) is like *aruṇā* (red). Thus, it is established that a qualification residing in the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), whereas one residing in the predicate (*upādeya*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). If it is argued: "In this way, since it is possible to enjoin—by means of the word *citrayā* (with the variegated [cow])—the instrumentality of the animal qualified by both variegation and femininity within the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice which is restated by the word *yajeta* (one should sacrifice), how can it not be a name (*nāmadheya*)? [The answer is: No.

If that were the case, there would be an abandonment of the sacrifice to Prajāpati under discussion, which requires a connection with a fruit, and the assumption of an unrelated sacrifice to Agni-Soma. Both of these are improper; therefore, the word *citrayā* is the name of a ritual action. In this manner, the status of a ritual name (*karmanāmadheya*) is to be inferred everywhere through one or another of these criteria, such as "being known from that" (*tatprakhya*). Thus, the authority of the injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) has been examined.
Now follows the examination of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*).

Now, the *arthavāda* (explanatory passages) are examined. Since explanatory passages lack a purpose in being restricted to their own literal meaning, it is necessary—by virtue of the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*)—that they serve the purpose of producing knowledge of a fruitful meaning. Their authority is established through syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhyekavākyatā*), by means of conveying the excellence (*prāśastya*) pertaining to that which is to be enjoined. Furthermore, that [authority] is fourfold, based on the distinctions of censure (*nindā*), praise (*praśaṃsā*), "deeds of others" (*parakṛti*), and "ancient events" (*purākalpa*).

In this regard, an explanatory passage of censure (*nindārthavāda*) is as follows: "That which is without a *chandoma* is indeed without a sacrificial session (*asatra*)," and "Silver is born of tears; he who gives silver upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) will have weeping in his house before a year has passed," and so forth. An explanatory passage of praise (*praśaṃsā*) is as follows: "The face of one who knows thus shines," and "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own portion, and he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity," and so forth.

*Parakṛti* (the deed of another) is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that establishes that "this action was performed by another great person," such as "Agni, indeed, desired," and so forth. *Purākalpa* (ancient history) is an explanatory passage that establishes events narrated by others, such as "He cursed him; they would have slain you blow after blow," and so forth. Among these, an explanatory passage of censure has as its ultimate purpose the praise of the enjoined act, by means of censuring something other than that which is to be enjoined.

In the case of the passage beginning with "aśrujam," since there is no contradiction when it aims to praise the prohibition of giving silver—which is the object of the injunction—by means of a censure of silver, the other three [passages] likewise aim directly at praising the injunction itself. Regarding the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "Vāyur vai," because Vāyu is extremely praiseworthy as a deity due to his swift movement, the ritual action dedicated to him is also praiseworthy; thus, through the presentation of the praise inherent in the deity who is the object of the injunction, it forms a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction.

Regarding the statement, "Agni indeed desired," the sacrifice dedicated to Agni is praised because it was performed by Agni in former times; thus, out of devotion, it must necessarily be performed even now by other sacrificers. Therefore, through the praise inherent in the enjoined act, there is syntactic unity with the injunction (*vidhyekavākyatva*). This should be inferred similarly in other cases as well. In some instances, however, there is also another function; for example, in the injunction, "He places the smeared pebbles," the word "smeared" (*aktāḥ*) conveys a general liquid substance.

When there arises the doubt as to what that substance might be, it is determined to be clarified butter (*ghṛta*) on the basis of the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*): "Clarified butter is indeed light" (*tejo vai ghṛtam*). Thus, the authority of the explanatory passage "Clarified butter is indeed light" consists in its capacity to determine a doubtful meaning. This concludes the investigation of explanatory passages. Now follows the investigation of mantras.

Now, the consideration of mantras: even for mantras, by virtue of the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the entire Veda has as its purpose the knowledge of the meaning that yields fruit, and not an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*). For when a visible purpose is possible, it is improper to postulate an unseen one. Since at the time of performance, the execution of a rite is impossible without knowledge of that rite, the knowledge of the meaning conducive to the rite is produced by the mantras. Nor should it be argued that the performance of the rite is possible because the recollection of the meaning can occur through the words of an instructor and so forth.

Because it is accepted as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that a result arises only when the performance is carried out after recollecting the meaning by means of the mantras themselves, and not otherwise; because an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is necessarily accepted through that restriction; and because it is postulated that in the absence of that [recollected meaning], the resulting unseen merit would be lost, and consequently the fruit rooted in it would not be accomplished. [Objection: If this is so, the conclusion is that mantras are employed (*viniyoga*) with respect to an object that they themselves manifest. Employment (*viniyoga*) is indeed connection as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). And subordination (*śeṣatva*) is nothing other than being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*).

Furthermore, if it is asked: "Since the mantra *imāmagṛbhṇan raśanām* possesses the capacity for grasping the rope, its status as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the grasping of the rope is established by the indicative power (*liṅga*)—namely, the capacity to manifest the act of grasping the rope—then what is the purpose of the scriptural statement (*vacana*), *'imāmagṛbhṇan raśanāmṛtasyetyaśvābhidhānīmādatte'* (he takes up the horse's halter with the mantra *imāmagṛbhṇan...*)," the answer is: No, because it serves the purpose of exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*). Within the context of the fire-altar construction (*cayana-prakaraṇa*), there are two acts: the grasping of the horse's halter and the grasping of the donkey's halter.

In this context, when it is stated that the mantra is obtained for the horse’s halter by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*), the mantra would also apply to the donkey’s halter because the indicative power is non-distinct. Therefore, this injunction—stating that the mantra should be used only for the horse’s halter and not for the donkey’s halter—is intended as a restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) whose purpose is the exclusion of the mantra from the donkey’s halter.
Regarding this restrictive enumeration, there are three types of defects.

And that enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) consists of three defects (*tridoṣā*), due to the distinctions of: abandonment of one's own meaning (*svārthatyāga*), acceptance of another’s meaning (*parārthasvīkāra*), and sublation of what has been obtained (*prāptabādha*). In the sentence "He takes up the horse's halter," the literal meaning of this mantra is that "one should perform the taking up of the horse's tether with this mantra"; that [meaning] is abandoned. The exclusion of the mantra from the donkey's tether is the purpose of another; that is accepted. Furthermore, there is the sublation of the mantra which would otherwise be obtained for the donkey's tether by virtue of its indicative power (*liṅga*)—thus, enumeration involving these three defects is accepted because there is no other way [to avoid them]. If another way were possible, it would not be appropriate. This is *vikalpa* (option).

Thus, even this conceptual construction (vikalpa), though flawed by eight defects and leaving one with no other recourse, has been accepted. For example: when it is understood that the *puroḍāśa*—an offering of eight potsherds prepared from grain—is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the sacrifice, there arises an expectancy for a material cause (*prakṛtidravya*) for that specific cake, the *puroḍāśa*. In the absence of a restrictive rule, any material whatsoever might be obtained; however, by the sentence "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), rice is restricted. Likewise, by the sentence "one should sacrifice with barley" (*yavair yajeta*), barley is also restricted. Since these two serve the same purpose, they stand in a relationship of option (*vikalpa*).

Thus, in the statement "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*," the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* is prescribed for the *atirātra*. Likewise, by the prohibition "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* at the *atirātra*," the absence of taking it is prescribed. Since these two—the taking and the non-taking—which are mutually contradictory, cannot be performed in a single performance (*prayoga*), there must be the performance of taking in one performance and the performance of its absence in another; thus, even in that case, there is an option (*vikalpa*). Regarding this option, there are eight defects.

And that [scripture] is vitiated by eight defects. To explain: first, in the application regarding rice, there is the abandonment of the validity of the *yava* (barley) scripture—characterized by its capacity to prompt the performance of its own injunction—and the acceptance of its invalidity—characterized by its incapacity to prompt performance. Then, in the second application, upon the performance of barley, there is the acceptance of that validity which was previously abandoned and the abandonment of that invalidity which was previously accepted. Thus, there are four defects in the *yava* scripture.

Thus, in the first performance using barley, there is the abandonment of the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the rice-scripture (*vrīhi-śāstra*), which consists in its capacity to bring about its own object; and there is the acceptance of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), which consists in its incapacity to bring about that object. Then, in the second performance when rice is used, there is the acceptance of the authority of the rice-scripture that was previously abandoned, and the abandonment of the lack of authority that was previously accepted. Thus, there are four faults regarding the rice-scripture; this constitutes an option (*vikalpa*) corrupted by eight faults. And such an option occurs only in some cases, because of the identity of purpose (*ekārthatva*).

The meaning is: because they accomplish a single purpose. For example, there is an option between rice (*vrīhi*) and barley (*yava*), since each one individually is capable of producing the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). In some cases, it is by the force of a scriptural statement; for instance, "The *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*" prescribes a hymn named *pṛṣṭha* to be accomplished by the *bṛhat* Sāman, while "The *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha*" prescribes another *pṛṣṭha* hymn to be accomplished by the *rathantara* Sāman. And this hymn, like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, is a primary act (*arthakarma*) because it serves the purpose of producing the unseen potency (*apūrva*).

The *sāman*, however, is a subordinate action (*guṇakarma*) because its function is one of refinement (*saṃskārakarmatva*). This is because it is accepted that the *sāmans* serve as the means for the *stotra* by way of the refinement consisting in the manifestation of the syllables of the *stotrīyā* verses which constitute the *stotra*. A *stotra* is the declaration of qualities residing in a subject such as Indra, accomplished by means of a chanted mantra; the meaning is that it is accomplished by the syllables of a *ṛc* verse manifested by a *sāman* through a chanted mantra. A *śastra* is the declaration of qualities residing in a subject accomplished by means of a non-chanted mantra. A *sāman* is a specific type of the act of singing.

The *ṛc* verses that serve as the means for a hymn of praise (*stotra*) are called *stotrīyās*. The specific numbers such as ninefold (*trivṛt*), fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), and so forth, are the *stomas*; this is the distinction between them. Thus, although the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* *pṛṣṭha* chants have different *apūrva*s (transcendental results) and lack a single common purpose, there is nonetheless an option (*vikalpa*) based solely on the force of the scriptural injunction: "Either the *Bṛhat* *pṛṣṭha* should be performed, or the *Rathantara* *pṛṣṭha* should be performed. In some cases, the option is restricted (*vyavasthitavikalpa*).

In the ritual acts such as the second *prayāja*, there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the *nārāśaṃsa* and *tanūnapāt* mantras because they serve the same purpose. And since that option is regulated by the statement, "For the *rājanya*s, the *vasiṣṭha*s, and others, the second *prayāja* is the *nārāśaṃsa*; for others, it is the *tanūnapāt*," it is a "regulated option" (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*).
The entire Veda possesses authority regarding the objects known as dharma and adharma.

Thus, since injunctive sentences—synonymous with *codanā*—possess authority because they enjoin a *bhāvanā* (productive activity) qualified by the three factors [the end, the means, and the procedure], and since terms such as *udbhid* possess authority as names (*nāmadheya*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) as being intent upon praising what is enjoined, and mantras as being reminders of the objects to be performed, the authority of the entire Veda regarding the non-worldly objects known as *dharma* and *adharma* is established. This concludes the investigation into the authority of the Veda. Now begins the investigation into the authority of the Smṛtis and other sources.

Since the Smṛtis composed by Manu and others are also rooted in the Veda, they possess authority regarding dharma such as the Aṣṭakā rites. However, the Smṛti rule "The Audumbarī post must be entirely covered" is not authoritative, because it contradicts the direct Vedic Śruti: "Having touched the Audumbarī, one should sing. For if it were entirely covered, the touching prescribed by the Śruti would be impossible to perform.

The Smṛti text, "The Adhvaryu takes the garment used for the Vaisarjana oblation," and so forth, is not authoritative, because it is rooted in greed even though it does not contradict the meaning of the Śruti. Likewise, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is authoritative because it is rooted in the Śruti through the medium of Smṛti. However, the conduct of the learned regarding such matters as marrying the daughter of one's maternal uncle is not authoritative. [As it is said: "One who has married the daughter of his maternal uncle, as well as one who has married a girl of his mother’s gotra..."

Because [marrying] one who has the same *pravara* is prohibited by such Smṛti texts as, "Having abandoned her who possesses that [same *pravara*, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance," it is contrary to Smṛti. Thus, the authority of Śruti, Smṛti, and custom regarding dharma and adharma has been stated.
These are the means of knowledge that mutually differentiate dharma.

And that dharma is mutually distinct; the means of proof for this distinction are, for instance, synonyms and so forth. To illustrate: there is a distinction between sacrifice (*yajati*), giving (*dadāti*), and offering (*juhoti*) due to their being conveyed by different words (*śabdāntara*), as they are expressed by non-synonymous terms. Giving (*dāna*) consists in the transfer of ownership to another, preceded by the cessation of one's own ownership.

Among the five sentences beginning with "He offers the *samidhs*," since there is no determining factor to establish that one of them is the injunction of an action while the others are injunctions of accessories (*guṇa*) for that same action, it follows that all of them are injunctions of actions. Once this is established, the re-injunction of an action already enjoined would be purposeless; therefore, by the force of this re-injunction, the difference between each subsequent action enjoined by the successive sentences—relative to the action enjoined by the preceding sentence—is established. Such is the [argument].

Furthermore, in cases where there is no distinction in the context (*sthala*), a difference in action arises from the repetition of a word in the form of a scriptural injunction (*śruti*), such as the repeated term "he sacrifices" (*yajati*). In the case of "He offers three oblations" (*tisra āhutīr juhoti*), although there is no repetition of the word "he offers" (*juhoti*), because the number three is connected to the oblation—which is the meaning of *juhoti*—there are three mutually distinct oblations; thus, here the difference in action is established by number (*saṃkhyā*).

"Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis; one should sacrifice with this [rite] in which a thousand is the sacrificial fee"—since these three sacrifices named Jyotis, though heard within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, are given distinct names apart from the name "Jyotiṣṭoma," there is a difference from the Jyotiṣṭoma. Precisely because of these distinct names, there is a mutual difference among the three; thus, there is a difference of ritual acts (*karmabheda*) based on the name.

Likewise, in the passage, "He pours curds into hot milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas; the *vājina* for the Vājins," the sentence "that is for the Viśvedevas" (*sā vaiśvadevī*) enjoins a sacrifice inferred from the relationship between the Viśvedeva deities and the *āmikṣā* substance. In the phrase "the *vājina* for the Vājins" (*vājibhyo vājinam*), a separate ritual action characterized by the Vājins as deities and the *vājina* as its substance is enjoined. It is not the case that the quality of the *vājina* substance is enjoined as an attribute within the previously enjoined Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.

Because the previous sacrifice is already occupied by the quality of *āmikṣā* (curd-mixture), there is no possibility for the *vājina* (whey) to be inserted therein. Nor can there be an option between the two, as in the case of rice and barley, because *vājina* and *āmikṣā* are not enjoined equally. An option is impossible between two things that are enjoined unequally. In the very originative statement (*utpattivākya*) of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the quality of *āmikṣā* is enjoined; "enjoined" (*śiṣṭa*) means it is taught or prescribed. This is therefore an "originally enjoined" (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) element.

When a ritual action has been produced by the sentence concerning the Vaiśvadeva, the quality of *vājina* (whey) enjoined by another sentence is "enjoined subsequent to production" (*utpannaśiṣṭa*). Between these two, that which is "enjoined at the time of production" (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) is stronger, because it is established as an integral part of the ritual action at the very moment the action itself is being produced.

The quality of *vājina* (the whey remaining after curdling) is enjoined subsequently; although it is perceived immediately [after the milk], because it is delayed, it is weak and thus fails to find a place within the preceding ritual action. Consequently, due to its connection with a different deity in the form of *vājina*, it leads one's own sentence to enjoin a separate ritual action. This constitutes differentiation based on a quality (*guṇāt bhedaḥ*). In this context, the thickened milk is *āmikṣā*, while the remaining water is *vājina*. Similarly, in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "Having performed the *upasad* rites, he offers the *agnihotra* for a month."

In this case, no prior action whatsoever is present; rather, due to the "separation of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), which consists in the absence of the presence of a prior action, another distinct rite is enjoined—one that possesses the characteristics of the well-known *Agnihotra* and bears that same name. It is not, however, an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) by restating the well-known *Agnihotra* through the word *Agnihotra*. For if there were an injunction of multiple accessories—such as immediate sequence and the use of curd—in an action already established, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Thus, here there is a difference of action due to the separation of context.

The "well-known Agnihotra" refers to the obligatory Agnihotra, meaning the daily Agnihotra. Thus, the distinction between ritual acts (*karmabheda*) has been demonstrated through difference of words, repetition, number, name, quality, and difference of context. This concludes the determination of the distinction between ritual acts.

An Investigation of the Objects of Cognition (Prameya): Now follows the investigation of the objects of cognition and so forth. Among these, the object of cognition as established by the Vedas and other sources is threefold: that which subserves the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), that which subserves the person (*puruṣārtha*), and that which subserves both. Therein, the *prayāja* offerings and the like subserviently serve only the sacrifice; whereas the fruit and its means subserviently serve the person—such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and heaven, respectively.

Curd and the like, however, possess both forms: because of the statement "one should offer with curd," which—being unconnected to a specific fruit—is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*); yet because of the injunction "one desiring sensory power should offer with curd," it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*). As it has been said: "But when one thing has both forms, there is the principle of distinct connection (*saṃyogapṛthaktvam*). Connection refers to the sentence; its "distinctness" means its difference. And that [principle] is the regulator for when one thing serves both purposes. This concludes the investigation into the causal efficacy (*prayojakatva*).

In the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the like, which serve the purpose of a sacrifice (*ṛtu*), the sacrifice is the motivator (*prayojaka*). In the case of those serving the purpose of a person (*puruṣārtha*), the fruit is the motivator. "Motivator-ness" means the state of being that which causes performance; that is to say, for whatever purpose an injunction causes something to be performed, that [purpose] is the motivator therein. Since the injunction for the *darśa* and other sacrifices causes the *darśa* and so forth to be performed for the sake of heaven, heaven and the like are the motivators for the *darśa* and so forth. Since the injunction for the *prayāja* offerings causes the *prayāja* offerings to be performed for the sake of the *darśa* and so forth, the *darśa* and so forth are the motivators for the *prayāja* offerings.

The injunction for bringing curds (dadhyānayanavidhi) necessitates the performance of bringing curds for the sake of the *āmikṣā*, not for the sake of the *vājina*. This is because when the bringing of curds is performed for the sake of the *āmikṣā*, the *vājina* is established by itself.

Therefore, it is *āmikṣā* alone that motivates the bringing of curds, not the *vājina*. As for the injunction, "One scatters the husks with the cake-pan" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*), although the cake-pan is prescribed as a subsidiary to the scattering of husks, nevertheless, the scattering of husks does not become the motivator for the pan; for the scattering of husks is accomplished by means of the very pan already employed for the sake of the cake. Rather, it should be understood that the cake itself is the motivator for the pan, and so forth. This concludes the determination of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and other categories.

Now, the determination of sequence (*krama-nirūpaṇam*). Indeed, by means of an injunction (*vidhi*), the principal rite together with its subsidiaries is enjoined as something to be performed. Since there is a multiplicity of both subsidiary and principal actions therein, their performance must be stated to occur in a specific order. If it is asked, "What is the authority that determines that sequence?"—we reply: it is precisely *śruti* and the other authorities that determine the sequence. First, the sequence of *śruti* (*śruti-krama*).

To explain: in the passage, "Having initiated the householder (gṛhapati), he initiates the Brahman," the sequence of initiation for the Brahman immediately following that of the householder is established by the direct statement (*śruti*) of the suffix *-ktvā*; this is *śrauta-krama* (scriptural order). *Arthakrama* (logical order) is seen in the case of, "He offers the Agnihotra; he cooks the gruel. Since the cooking of the gruel is for the purpose of the oblation, and because the oblation cannot be performed before the cooking, one must set aside the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*) and accept the logical order. "Artha" means purpose, such as the oblation; the sequence for that purpose is *arthakrama*. Therefore, first comes the cooking, and afterwards the oblation.

The order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) refers to the sequence of performing sacrifices such as the *samit* and *tanūnapāt*, which follows precisely the order of the injunctive sentences, such as "he sacrifices the *samits*" and "he sacrifices the *tanūnapāt*. The order of position (*sthānakrama*) is as follows: in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, starting from the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*), three animals—the *āmīṣomīya*, the *savanīya*, and the *anubandhya*—are to be performed in succession. However, in the *Sādyaska* Soma sacrifice, it is enjoined that "one should immolate the animals together," which indicates simultaneity (*sāhitya*) in performance. This [simultaneity] is prescribed specifically in place of the *savanīya*.

In that context, setting aside the natural order (*prākṛtakrama*), because the performance of the *savanīya* animal sacrifice is prescribed as occurring simultaneously with the others at its own place, the sequence is determined by position (*sthāna*): first the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of the *savanīya* animal, then that of the *agnīṣomīya*, and then that of the *anūbandhyā*. The day preceding the day of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*) is the day of fasting (*aupavasathya*).
This is the sequence by principal (*mukhyakrama*).

Similarly, in the case of the *darśa* sacrifice, although the procedures for the *sāṃnāyya* (the milk offering), such as cutting the branch (*śākhāccheda*), occur first, and the procedures for the *āgneya* (the cake offering to Agni), such as the pouring out of the grain (*nirvāpa*), occur immediately thereafter; nevertheless, because the *āgneya* sacrifice is performed before the principal *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice, the sequence of the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) follows the order of the principal sacrifices: first the sprinkling of the remnants of the *āgneya* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and then the sprinkling of the milk. This is the sequence based on the order of the principal sacrifices, known as *pravṛttikrama*.

Likewise, in the case of the injunction, "One sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," seventeen sacrifices—characterized by seventeen animal-substances and having Prajāpati as their deity—are enjoined as things to be performed. Among these, the first ritual act, known as *upākaraṇa* (the preliminary dedication), may be commenced from any point and completed anywhere. However, subsequent acts such as *niyojana* (tying to the sacrificial post) must be performed in the very same order in which the *upākaraṇa* was initiated.

How so? In the archetype (*prakṛti*), since the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*anīṣomīyapaśu*) is a single entity, the preliminary rite (*upākaraṇa*) is performed first, followed by the tying (*niyojana*) in the very second moment, and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) in the third moment; this is because there is no cause for any interval between them. Here, however, because of the scriptural injunction that seventeen animals are to be performed together, the *upākaraṇa* performed first on any one animal may tolerate an interval of sixteen moments for the tying—which must be performed upon its own substrate—but not more than that.

In that regard, if one were to perform the tethering (*niyojana*) on the second animal first—rather than performing the tethering on the first animal according to the sequence of the preliminary rite (*upākaraṇa*)—and subsequently perform the tethering on the first animal, an interval of more than sixteen moments would result, which is not sanctioned by the scriptures. To avoid this, the tethering and subsequent rites must be performed in the very same order in which the preliminary rite was undertaken; this is the "order of commencement" (*pravṛttikrama*). Thus, the performance of rituals is governed precisely by the orders of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), purpose (*artha*), textual recitation (*pāṭha*), position (*sthāna*), principal action (*mukhya*), and commencement (*pravṛtti*).
If performed otherwise, there is a deficiency (*vaiguṇya*); so much for this.
Thus ends the *Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā* composed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa Yajvan.
